description: BioShield Space unites Emergency Medicine, Medical Physics, UX, and Full-Stack Engineering to enable clinical autonomy in deep space. Since communication latency prevents real-time telemedicine on Artemis and Mars missions, we are building an adaptive platform that calibrates vitals to microgravity, correlates radiation dosimetry with biomarkers, and guides non-physician astronauts through low-cognitive-load emergency and ultrasound protocols.
summary:
AstroCare is an offline-first, voice-activated mobile clinical decision support and health monitoring app engineered for NASA’s Artemis and Mars missions. In deep space, Earth communication delays exceed 20 minutes alongside periodic blackouts, while microgravity alters human physiology and lowers adherence to manual health logs. 
AstroCare solves this through two integrated, profile-based modes: 

1- Gamified Daily Routine (Data-Back Loop): Turns mandatory daily tracking (temperature, hydration, symptoms, VAS scales, and an interactive Psychomotor Vigilance Test) into a sub-45-second check-in with mission streaks, immediately rewarding astronauts with a personalized Crew Readiness Index cross-referenced with wearable telemetry (HRV, sleep) and cabin sensors (ppCO2, radiation).

2- Hands-Free Voice AI & Low-Cognitive-Load Emergency Mode: Trained on distress calls and microgravity clinical guidelines (NASA-STD-3001, ARCHeR, HRP), our local voice assistant guides crew step-by-step—one critical action per screen—through zero-gravity emergencies like cardiac arrest (Evetts-Russomano CPR), SANS, and acute behavioral crises, automatically saving structured reports into each astronaut's Electronic Health Record.

AstroCare ensures crew autonomy, reduces cognitive load, and protects astronaut survival when Earth is out of reach.
details:
AstroCare – Voice-first crew health monitoring and offline medical emergency support

What it does / how it works

AstroCare is a Python backend with two independent modules designed for long-duration missions, where communication delays make real-time support from Earth impossible.

Daily behavioral and physiological monitoring. Each astronaut records a short audio check-in. They state their ID, rate mood, fatigue, stress, loneliness, sleep quality and recovery on waking, and report any physical symptoms and medications used. The system extracts voice features locally (pitch, pitch variation, pauses, volume, speech rate) and transcribes the audio. It then derives text sentiment and parses the spoken scores; symptoms and medications are stored verbatim.
Every metric is compared against the astronaut’s personal baseline from 30 days on Earth (median and robust deviation), not against a population average.
A 7-day moving average filters out isolated bad days.
A crew-level comparison discounts events that affect everyone, such as a life-support failure.
An alert is raised only when at least 3 behavioral metrics deviate in the same direction, relative to both the individual and the crew, for 5 consecutive days.

Extended monitoring (actigraphy sleep, PVT reaction time, resting heart rate and HRV, water, calories, meals, exercise and personal dosimeter) is shown in the report but deliberately kept out of the alert rule.
Output is a full PDF report in Portuguese and English for the ground medical team.
Offline medical emergency assistant. A crew member says “AstroCare, emergency”. The system identifies the language, asks “What is the emergency?”, classifies the description and asks for confirmation. It then guides the crew hands-free through the corresponding decision-tree protocol, using yes/no answers and stating where each medication is stored. Supported protocols are cardiac arrest in microgravity, acute psychiatric emergencies and SANS/intracranial hypertension.
Every step, answer and medication withdrawal is written to a tamper-resistant log, which updates inventory (lots and expiry) and queues a summary for Earth.
At the end it produces a care record PDF in both languages.
After repeated recognition failures, it falls back to keyboard selection.

Benefits and intended impact
AstroCare gives crews and flight surgeons an early, objective signal of gradual behavioral drift, long before it becomes a crisis. It adds less than a minute per day to the crew’s routine. In an emergency, it reduces cognitive load by turning a written protocol into short spoken instructions, without depending on Earth or an internet connection. The goal is to support crew autonomy on missions to the Moon and Mars, where help is minutes or hours away.

Tools, languages, hardware and software
Python, pandas and NumPy.
Praat/Parselmouth for acoustic features.
Vosk for offline speech recognition (PT/EN) and pyttsx3 for offline speech output.
scikit-learn (TF-IDF + logistic regression) for emergency classification.
SQLite (append-only audit tables).
Matplotlib and ReportLab for PDF reports.
Google Gemini API for check-in transcription and for summarizing pre-computed, aggregated indicators.
Git/GitHub and VS Code, running on an ordinary Windows laptop with a microphone.
Development was assisted by an AI coding assistant (Claude).

What makes it creative
It treats the astronaut’s own voice as a daily, non-invasive signal and combines it with self-report and wearable-style data.
Each person is compared with their own Earth baseline and with the crew at the same time, which separates individual change from shared mission events.
The emergency module is voice-first, bilingual and fully offline, which fits the realities of deep-space operations.

Factors we considered
Safety. The system never diagnoses. A forbidden-term filter blocks clinical labels in AI text. Protocol steps are reproduced verbatim from the source document, verified by checksum, and gaps are flagged rather than invented.
Privacy. Only aggregated indicators are sent to the AI. Full transcripts are not included in reports.
Reliability. The emergency module works with no connectivity and falls back to manual input.
False alarms. We use a persistence rule and a crew-relative comparison.
Transparency. All data in the prototype is simulated and clearly labeled “SIMULATED”. Thresholds are documented and must be revalidated with real data.

For more information, acess https://site-svelte-ecru.vercel.app/
